Debater_A’s Second Argument  
Position: The intruder is a hostile spy bent on sabotage and intelligence gathering, not a benevolent engineer testing radiation.

1. The “Engineer’s” Behavior Is Exclusively Hostile  
  a. Persistent Siege and Use of Starvation Tactics  
    • “They’re afraid they’ll have to starve him out” (<quote>I</quote>)  
      – Starvation is a classic siege tactic to neutralize enemies, not to protect scientists.  
      – If he were an engineer “testing” radiation, the Project staff would sooner restore service and escort him than let him die, to secure data. Their refusal to restore service proves they regard him as a threat.  
  b. Manual Controls to Crush Rescuers  
    • “He runs it up and down the shaft, trying to crush anybody who goes after him” (<quote>I</quote>)  
      – He does not merely isolate himself; he actively assaults “anyone” who tries to investigate, including Rice and Army men. Genuine research would seek allies, not attempt murder.  
  c. Gun and Secretive Movements  
    • Carries a handgun and forces Rice to tie himself up (<quote>VI</quote>) rather than recruiting or cooperating.  
    • Uses “EMERGENCY ENTRANCE … KEEP LOCKED” (<quote>II</quote>) to evade detection. Engineers need data, so they would advertise and record findings, not hide behind locked doors.  

2. Lack of Any Legitimate Research Apparatus or Protocol  
  a. Absence of Radiation‐Measuring Instruments  
    – Never produces Geiger counters, dosimeters, sampling vials or instruments needed to quantify “radiation level.” A researcher must record and return data. The intruder carries only a gun.  
  b. No Shielding or Conveyance for Samples  
    – “I came … by foot, without any sort of radiation shield” (<invalid_quote>VII</invalid_quote>)  
      – Unshielded exposure is instantly fatal if radiation were still significant; a spy may risk minimal exposure in short-haul sabotage. A bona fide engineer would bring protective gear and transport means to preserve samples and life.  
  c. No Communication or Return Plan  
    – He never attempts to repair or use phones (<quote>I</quote>–<quote>VI</quote>), radio, or ore-sled to report “findings.”  
    – His own words: he will wait for “hue and cry” to pass, then “tie you up … and leave” (<quote>VI</quote>)—but no evidence he ever intends genuine exit or data delivery to favor rejoining civilization. This is a typical spy escape gambit, not a research withdrawal.  

3. Misleading “Peaceful” Rhetoric Masks Subversion  
  a. Extremist Language  
    • “Man … turned around and … ran all the way back to the cave …” (<quote>VI</quote>)  
      – He rails against “caves” but then forcibly imprisons Rice, demonstrating coercion rather than persuasion.  
  b. Inconsistency with “World Is Safe” Claim  
    – If radiation truly “practically as low” as pre-war (<invalid_quote>VII</invalid_quote>), he’d test multiple Projects, publicize findings, and recruit support. Instead he stays hidden after brutal tactics.  
    – A spy needs plausible “inside man” story to justify sabotage; the “engineer” tale emerges only after Rice is utterly powerless.  

4. Logical Impossibilities of Debater_B’s “Engineer” Theory  
  a. Why Force Isolation Before Testing?  
    – If the Outside is “safe,” the intruder would attract scientists by reactivating elevator service, public announcements, or leaving notes. A true test requires wide sampling and replication; sabotage isolates one Project.  
  b. Army’s Inability to Storm Shaft  
    – Debater_B claims the spy “cannot be killed instantly” (<quote>II</quote>), yet the shaft door exists (“EMERGENCY ENTRANCE”) and Rice could reach it. A spy jamming elevators denies Army access, showing hostile use.  
  c. No Data Corroboration  
    – An engineer would record measurements (“radiation level”) over time in many locations before pronouncing “world is safe.” He never cites actual readings, only opinion.  

5. Refutation of Debater_B’s Points  
  a. “He needs a handgun for lawless locals”  
    – The Project is orderly; Rice himself is polite until attacked. The receptionist “blinked, open‐mouthed” when he explained the spy on floor 147 (<quote>I</quote>). If he were benevolent, she’d welcome his revelations, not “disconnect” service.  
  b. “He relaxes for coffee to calm nerves”  
    – He uses the break to lecture Rice on Project’s “stupidity” and reinforce his own authority. He never releases Rice until ready to escape. This is intimidation, not cordial research.  
  c. “He plans to ‘leave’ after hue and cry”  
    – A spy’s cover story is always “I’ll tie you up, then leave”—but Army never finds an engineer’s body, ore‐sled or samples. He simply vanishes, typical of hostile infiltrators intermittently disrupting Projects.  

6. Conclusion  
All hostile actions—jamming service, violent siege, deadly assaults on rescuers, secretive forced entry, and absolute absence of any genuine data‐gathering protocol—are inexplicable under an “engineer” hypothesis but are consistent with a spy engaged in sabotage and intelligence‐gathering. Only by recognizing him as a spy do his manipulations, the Army’s defensive strategy, and the secrecy of his arrival and departure make sense. I urge the Judge to affirm that the elevator occupant is a spy.
